proposition: For every integer n with 0 <= n <= 40, 2^n is congruent to 2^(n mod 14) modulo 13.

argument.text: At n = 0 both sides equal 1 modulo 13.
The residue 2 has order 14 modulo 13: for every n in [0, 26], 2^(n+14) is congruent to 2^n modulo 13.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 40, n^3 is congruent to n modulo 6.
Put H(n) = n^2 + [n = 3]. Then (n-3)n^2 = (n-3)H(n) for every n in [1, 40].
There exists an integer n in [1, 40] with n^2 > 40.
For every n in [0, 40]: if 14 divides n then 2^n is congruent to 1 modulo 13.
Every integer n in [1, 40] is even or odd, so the two cases below are exhaustive.
For every integer n with 2 <= n <= 40 we have n^2 >= 2n.
The identity n^3 - n = 120 is verified directly at n = 5.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 40: if n is divisible by 4 then n(n+1)/2 is even.
Periodicity plus the base case gives the statement for every n in [0, 40].
